analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers prepare and file federal returns free through a permanent IRS-run online program.
analysis.headline: With all 40 Senate Democrats and independents backing it, the bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no vote since the day it was introduced in February 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write the IRS Direct File program into law, making free online tax preparation and filing a permanent, government-owned service rather than something a future administration could end on its own. It would bar the Treasury Department from signing any agreement that limits the government's right to offer tax filing services, and would void any such agreement already in place within 30 days. It requires the program to import data the IRS already has, be accessible on phones, be offered in multiple languages, and be promoted heavily, with no fee for users. States that integrate their own tax filing would get grants and their residents could file federal and state returns together.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary filers, especially people with simple returns who now pay commercial tax preparation fees or buy filing software each spring. The bill sets no user fee, and by locking the program into statute it protects the service from being discontinued by a future administration. Residents of states that join the program could file federal and state returns in one place.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday taxpayers who pay to file

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Treasury Secretary to establish and permanently operate a federal program where taxpayers can prepare and file income tax returns online, at no fee [S2].
The program must be government-owned, import IRS data to pre-fill returns, work on mobile devices, be available in multiple languages, and be promoted through a mass marketing campaign [S2].

It forbids the Treasury Secretary from entering any agreement that restricts the government's right to provide tax preparation and filing services, and voids existing agreements of that kind 30 days after enactment [S2].
For taxable years after 2027, at least half of taxpayers in participating states must be eligible, and the Secretary must keep expanding eligibility as far as possible [S2].
States that integrate their filing systems receive $1 million grants, and their residents can file state returns alongside federal ones [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and software companies would lose filing revenue to a free government alternative. The federal government would fund the program through appropriations, with funding authorized 'as necessary' for fiscal years 2026 through 2035, meaning an open-ended cost to taxpayers generally. Employers and other payers would face earlier deadlines for sending out information returns like W-2s.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tax software companies and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The program's reach is limited: only residents of states that choose to integrate state filing (or that have no income tax) are covered, and the requirement that at least half of those states' taxpayers be eligible only applies to years after 2027 [S2].
Funding is an open-ended authorization rather than a fixed budget, so the eventual cost to taxpayers is not defined in the bill [S2].
The bill moves most electronically filed information return deadlines to March 31, which shifts compliance work onto employers and other payers who issue W-2s and similar forms [S2].

Critics of government-run filing argue it puts the agency that writes tax rules in the position of competing with the private companies it regulates, and concentrates taxpayers' financial data in one government system; the industry has made this case for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For filers, the benefit is direct and easy to see: free filing replaces fees that run from a few dollars to well over a hundred for commercial software and preparation, and pre-filling from IRS data saves hours. The costs are real but narrower: an open-ended federal appropriation, earlier paperwork deadlines for employers, and lost revenue for tax prep companies. The main design weakness is that the guarantee of coverage only covers participating states and starts in earnest after 2027, so the initial reach is smaller than the bill's name implies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee has taken no action since; no vote has ever been scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Warren on February 26, 2026 and was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1][S4].

It would add a new section to the tax code establishing a permanent, free, government-owned online filing program, and would void agreements that restrict the government's right to provide filing services [S2].
Forty senators — 38 of 45 Democrats and both independents — cosponsored the bill [S3].
The action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote after the referral; the bill has remained with the Finance Committee since February 2026 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so the status quo continues: commercial tax preparation companies keep their filing fees, and taxpayers who would have used a free program keep paying. The administration's decision to wind down the existing Direct File pilot stands unchallenged in law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Commercial tax software companies, for now

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 40 cosponsors from her party and the independents.

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; his committee's Democratic side did not control its calendar.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, putting party leadership behind it.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction; the committee has taken no action on the bill since.

against.name: John Thune
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the Senate floor; no floor action appears in its history.

against.name: Tax preparation software industry
against.role: Commercial filing companies (TurboTax, H&R Block and peers)
against.what_they_did: For years operated a partnership with the IRS that limited the government's own filing services, and has lobbied against free government filing programs that compete with paid products.

against.name: Treasury Department and IRS under President Trump
against.what_they_did: Moved to wind down the existing Direct File pilot program that this bill would make permanent.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on, and Republicans chair the Finance Committee and hold 55 of 100 Senate seats.

industries.industry: Tax preparation software and services (Intuit, H&R Block and peers)
industries.note: A permanent, free, government-run filing program directly competes with the fees these companies charge tens of millions of filers each year. The bill also voids agreements — the long-standing Free File arrangement is the leading example — in which the government promised not to offer its own filing services, which is why the industry's interest in this bill runs against filers' savings.

industries.industry: Employers and other issuers of information returns
industries.note: The bill moves most electronic information return deadlines (W-2s and the like) to March 31, adding compliance work for payers. The change is designed to get data to the IRS earlier so returns can be pre-filled, which helps filers more than it hurts payers.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and the chair of the Finance Committee taking no action for months, the bill is very likely to die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027, unless it is attached to a larger tax or government-funding bill.
